subject: economics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The law of demand states that, ceteris paribus, as the price of a good rises, quantity demanded:
questions.explain: There is an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded.

questions.q: A change in the price of a good itself causes a:
questions.explain: Only a price change moves along the curve; non-price determinants shift the whole curve.

questions.q: An increase in consumer income for a normal good will:
options: Shift the demand curve to the right
questions.explain: Higher income raises demand for normal goods at every price, shifting the curve rightward.

questions.q: The law of supply states that, ceteris paribus, as price rises, quantity supplied:
questions.explain: Higher prices make production more profitable, so more is supplied.

questions.q: Market equilibrium occurs where:
questions.explain: At the equilibrium price there is no shortage or surplus; the market clears.

questions.q: If the market price is above equilibrium, there will be:
questions.explain: Above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, creating a surplus that pushes price down.

questions.q: A shortage (excess demand) tends to cause the price to:
questions.explain: Excess demand bids the price up until the market clears.

questions.q: Price elasticity of demand (PED) measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in:
questions.explain: PED = %change in quantity demanded / %change in price.

questions.q: If PED is greater than 1 (in magnitude), demand is described as:
questions.explain: Elastic demand means quantity responds more than proportionately to a price change.

questions.q: A good with few substitutes and that is a necessity tends to have demand that is:
questions.explain: Necessities with few substitutes show little quantity response to price changes.

questions.q: If a firm raises its price and total revenue falls, demand for its product is:
questions.explain: When demand is elastic, a price rise reduces quantity by proportionately more, lowering total revenue.

questions.q: Income elasticity of demand (YED) for an inferior good is:
questions.explain: For inferior goods, demand falls as income rises, giving a negative YED.

questions.q: Price elasticity of supply (PES) measures the responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in:
questions.explain: PES = %change in quantity supplied / %change in price; supply is more elastic when producers can respond easily.

questions.q: A price ceiling set below the equilibrium price will cause:
questions.explain: A binding maximum price (e.g. rent control) leads to excess demand as quantity demanded exceeds supply.

questions.q: A minimum price (price floor) set above equilibrium, such as a minimum wage, tends to create:
options: A surplus (e.g. unemployment in labour markets)
questions.explain: A binding price floor causes quantity supplied to exceed quantity demanded, creating a surplus.

questions.q: An indirect tax on a good shifts the:
questions.explain: A per-unit tax raises producers' costs, shifting supply up and increasing the market price.

questions.q: A government subsidy to producers will typically:
options: Lower the price and increase the quantity traded
questions.explain: Subsidies reduce production costs, shifting supply right, lowering price and raising quantity.

questions.q: A negative production externality (e.g. pollution) means that:
options: The social cost exceeds the private cost
The good is a public good
questions.explain: External costs imposed on third parties make social cost greater than private cost, causing overproduction.

questions.q: A public good is characterised by being:
questions.explain: Public goods (e.g. street lighting) suffer the free-rider problem, so markets under-provide them.

questions.q: At the socially optimal level of output, welfare is maximised where:
options: Marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost
questions.explain: Allocative efficiency (social optimum) occurs where MSB = MSC.

questions.q: A positive consumption externality, such as vaccination, tends to be:
questions.explain: Because private benefit is below social benefit, the market under-consumes goods with positive externalities.

questions.q: Total revenue is maximised when demand is:
questions.explain: Revenue peaks where PED equals 1, as further price changes reduce revenue on one side or the other.
